subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: The local bus from Kherwadi stopped at every tea stall, and Naveen didn't mind; back home, a meeting at ten meant somewhere near eleven. He reached the seed-trial farm at ten-thirty, sweating, pickle still on his fingers. Siddharth was waiting at the gate, face tight. "She started at ten sharp," he whispered. "Dr. Lena from the Dutch team asked twice where you were. Then she wrote something in her notebook." Inside, Dr. Lena gave Naveen a polite nod and handed the soil samples to Siddharth instead. Naveen's ears burned. That evening, on the bench at the bus stop, Siddharth explained that where she came from, half an hour late meant you did not care. Naveen had not meant that at all. The next week the bus broke down near the canal. At 9:40 he sent a message: "Bus stuck, reaching by 10:20, very sorry." Dr. Lena replied, "Thank you for telling me. We will start with the maps."

qa.q: What time did Naveen reach the seed-trial farm the first time?
qa.a: He reached the seed-trial farm at ten-thirty, sweating, with pickle still on his fingers.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when Dr. Lena handed the soil samples to Siddharth instead?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt; his ears burned because he could see she now doubted he could be relied on, though he had meant no disrespect.

qa.q: What small step helped Naveen the second time he was running late?
qa.a: He sent a message twenty minutes before the start with a new arrival time and an apology, so Dr. Lena could plan instead of wondering whether he cared.

qa.q: How might Dr. Lena have seen Naveen's first late arrival?
qa.a: In her way of working, turning up half an hour late without a word looked like not caring about the work, so she gave the task to Siddharth.

grounding: Shows a student used to loose timings arriving half an hour late to a strict-time meeting, being judged unreliable, and then warning ahead the next time.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: The weaving shed in the little town smelled of wet indigo when Elizabeth walked through with Pallavi's sample book. "These borders are uneven. The colour chart is wrong on page three. This will not pass the buyer." She said it flatly, then moved on to the looms. Pallavi stood holding the book, throat tight. Two years of work, and not one good word. Walking home past the pond she almost cried, then remembered her mother saying, "Ask first, sulk later." Next morning she found Elizabeth at the chai stall. "Yesterday felt harsh to me. Were you unhappy with my work overall?" Elizabeth looked surprised. "No! Your patterns are the best we have. Where I grew up, we say problems straight so they get fixed fast. I should have told you the good part too." Pallavi opened the book again. The borders really were uneven. That part, she decided, she could fix by Friday.

qa.q: Which page of the sample book had the wrong colour chart?
qa.a: The colour chart was wrong on page three.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel standing in the shed after Elizabeth's comments?
qa.a: She felt hurt and unappreciated; her throat went tight and she nearly cried on the way home because she heard not one good word after two years of work.

qa.q: What worked about the way Pallavi handled the criticism the next day?
qa.a: She asked Elizabeth what she meant instead of guessing, found out the blunt words were about the borders and not her worth, and kept the useful part to fix by Friday.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see her own blunt comments once Pallavi asks?
qa.a: Elizabeth is surprised, because to her plain words are simply a fast way to fix problems, and she sees she should have mentioned the good work too.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional hurt by a foreign manager's blunt criticism who asks about intent and separates the tone from the useful content.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: The naming ceremony started at eight, and at seven Irawati was still ironing a kurta in her rented room in Kumasi. Jyoti, her flatmate, was already at the door. "Just wear anything and take a box of sweets, it's fine." Irawati hesitated. At an office party last month she had held out her left hand to shake and watched a colleague's smile freeze. She knocked on her landlady's door instead. "Auntie Ama, quick question. Three, actually." Ama laughed and counted on her fingers: greet the elders first, use the right hand only, and a small gift for the baby is kinder than sweets. "And that colour is good. Not black, that is for funerals." They reached twenty minutes late, but Irawati went straight to the grandmother first, right hand held out. The old woman took it in both of hers and pulled Irawati down to a seat in the front row.

qa.q: Whose door did Irawati knock on before the ceremony?
qa.a: She knocked on her landlady's door and asked Auntie Ama.

qa.q: Why did Irawati hesitate when Jyoti told her to wear anything and take sweets?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and cautious, because she remembered a colleague's smile freezing when she offered her left hand, and she did not want to cause offence again.

qa.q: Which choice paid off at the ceremony, and why?
qa.a: Taking a few minutes to ask Auntie Ama, even though it made them late, meant Irawati greeted the grandmother first with her right hand and was welcomed to a front seat.

qa.q: How might the grandmother at the ceremony see Irawati?
qa.a: She likely saw a newcomer who had bothered to learn their ways and showed respect, which is why she held Irawati's hand in both of hers.

grounding: Shows a worker abroad asking a local about greetings, gifts and dress before assuming, and the warmth that humility wins.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Sabina's Sunday call to Lucknow could be heard from the stairwell. "Haan Ammi, I ate! No, not married yet, stop!" In the kitchen of their Melbourne flat, Chloe paused with the kettle, eyebrows up. Avni noticed. Last night Sabina had asked Chloe how much her new job paid and whether her boyfriend planned to propose, and Chloe had laughed too brightly and changed the subject. Later Sabina had wobbled her head at Chloe's question about dinner, and Chloe had waited, unsure if that meant yes. After the call, Avni made three cups of tea. "Chloe, where we grew up, lots of people ask about pay and marriage to show they care. And that head wobble usually means yes." Chloe grinned. "Good to know. I thought I'd offended her." Later Avni told Sabina gently, "Here those questions feel private. Maybe take Ammi's calls on the balcony?" Sabina rolled her eyes, then carried her phone outside.

qa.q: What did Sabina ask Chloe the night before?
qa.a: Sabina asked Chloe how much her new job paid and whether her boyfriend planned to propose.

qa.q: What might Avni have been worried about as she watched Chloe in the kitchen?
qa.a: Avni was uneasy that Chloe felt awkward and intruded on, and that her two flatmates were quietly misreading each other.

qa.q: How did Avni help both flatmates, and what made it work?
qa.a: She explained Sabina's habits kindly to Chloe and quietly suggested one small change to Sabina, so nobody felt blamed and both could adjust a little.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel about being asked to take calls on the balcony?
qa.a: Sabina may feel a bit annoyed or self-conscious, as the eye-roll shows, yet still goes outside, showing a willingness to adapt.

grounding: Shows a young Indian abroad noticing how personal questions, a head wobble and loud calls surprise a host, then explaining kindly so both sides adapt.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: At snack time in the Bandra playschool, Maria pushed her biscuit box away from the new boy. "People from the basti are lazy," she said, chin up. "Papa says." Miss Elizabeth knelt beside her. "Hmm. How do you know, Maria?" Maria blinked. She looked at Raju, who had tidied every block in the corner that morning, all by himself. "Papa says," she said again, more quietly. "Did you see Raju being lazy?" Maria shook her head slowly. Then she slid one biscuit across the table to him.

qa.q: What had Raju done that morning?
qa.a: Raju had tidied every block in the corner that morning, all by himself.

qa.q: How can you tell Maria began to feel unsure about what she said?
qa.a: She blinked, said "Papa says" more quietly, and shook her head slowly, so she seems confused and less certain than when she spoke with her chin up.

qa.q: What made Miss Elizabeth's question helpful?
qa.a: She calmly asked how Maria knew instead of scolding, which let Maria see she had only her father's words and no real reason.

qa.q: What is it like for Raju when Maria pushes her biscuit box away?
qa.a: He is shut out for something he never did, which could leave him feeling hurt and unwelcome at snack time.

grounding: Shows a young child repeating a label about a group heard at home, with no evidence of her own, and a teacher's calm how-do-you-know question.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage:
Monday. On the school bus, Kabir put on an accent, stretching his vowels like Mridula, the new girl from Kolkata. Everyone roared. Seema laughed loudest; it felt good to be inside the circle. Only Gurleen looked out of the window.
Wednesday. Kabir did it again at lunch. Seema started to giggle, then saw Mridula two tables away, staring hard at her tiffin. Gurleen said quietly, "Not funny, yaar," and went to sit with Mridula. Seema's cheeks went hot. She stayed where she was.
Friday. When Kabir began, Seema just kept eating. Nobody noticed much. After lunch she walked over and asked Mridula about the sweet in her tiffin. Mridula smiled a little and broke it in half to share.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen go after saying the joke was not funny?
qa.a: Gurleen went to sit with Mridula.

qa.q: Why did Seema laugh loudest on Monday?
qa.a: Laughing along made her feel included, safe inside the circle of friends, even though the joke was about Mridula.

qa.q: What small step did Seema take on Friday, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She stopped laughing and later went to ask Mridula about her sweet, which showed Mridula that not everyone was against her.

qa.q: What is it like for Mridula when the table laughs at the accent?
qa.a: She is likely hurt and lonely, staring at her tiffin while others laugh at the way she talks.

grounding: Shows a child laughing at accent jokes to belong, noticing the hurt of the classmate present, and following a friend who does not laugh.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage:
Day one of the chemistry project, Rohan grinned at Charu. "You're from Patna, so you'll just mug up the answers, na? All Biharis do." The others laughed. Charu laughed too, then spent the bus ride home staring at her own reflection in the window, feeling like a word instead of a person.
Three days later, the group divided tasks. Rohan handed her note-taking again. Charu's hands shook, but she said, "I'm actually good at the experiment part. I built the working model at my old school." Rohan shrugged. "Okay, okay, sorry." It sounded thin.
The next week, Deepika saved her a seat in the lab. "Your titration was the cleanest in the class," she said. "Want to prepare for the practical exam together?" Charu nodded, and for the first time since moving to Pune, she talked through the whole period.

qa.q: Which city is Charu from?
qa.a: Charu is from Patna.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling on the bus ride home after the first day?
qa.a: She felt hurt and unseen, like a word instead of a person, even though she had laughed along in the group.

qa.q: What helped Charu stop being boxed in by the label?
qa.a: Gently correcting Rohan by naming her real strength, and then finding a supportive classmate in Deepika, who noticed her actual work.

qa.q: How does Deepika see Charu, compared with Rohan?
qa.a: Deepika sees her as an individual with skills, praising her clean titration, while Rohan saw only where she came from.

grounding: Shows a teenager labelled by her home state, feeling unseen, then gently correcting it and finding a supportive peer.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: Friday film night at Ingrid's flat in Oslo had become a ritual: popcorn, one blanket, whatever the streaming menu offered. Halfway through a heist film, Emeka muttered, "Guess who dies first." The only African character was shot in the second scene. Ingrid laughed, then stopped. She thought of last week's comedy, where the Asian shopkeeper existed only for jokes, and the week before, where the maid never even had a name. She paused the film. "Is it always like that?" Emeka shrugged, not looking at her. "Pretty much." Ingrid pulled out a notebook, and for the next three films she wrote down who got lines, who got names, who got to be the hero. By the third film, the list made her quiet. "Who's missing?" she asked. Emeka finally smiled. "Now you're watching properly."

qa.q: What did Ingrid write down in her notebook?
qa.a: She wrote down who got lines, who got names, and who got to be the hero.

qa.q: Why did Ingrid go quiet by the third film?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and troubled because her list showed a clear pattern of who was left out or made into a joke, something she had laughed at before.

qa.q: What habit could Ingrid keep when she watches films?
qa.a: She can keep asking who is missing from the story and who gets names and lines, so she spots patterns instead of just soaking them up.

qa.q: What might it be like for Emeka to watch the only African character die first?
qa.a: Emeka seems tired of it, shrugging and saying "Pretty much" without looking up, and is pleased when Ingrid starts to notice too.

grounding: Shows a teenager noticing that films cast certain groups as victims, servants or jokes, and beginning to ask who is missing.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage:
"Wasim, you're home early."
"Class got cancelled. Why do you look like that?"
"Like what?"
"Like you swallowed a lemon, Afreen."
"Okay. On the metro there was this guy. Ripped jeans, tattoos up his neck, music blasting. I moved my bag to my other side and stood by the door."
"And?"
"My purse fell out when I got off. He ran after me across the platform to give it back. Said, 'Didi, your stuff.' Then he just left."
"So he was nice."
"He was nice. And I'd already decided he was a thief. Just from his clothes. That's what's bothering me."
"You're making a face like you robbed a bank."
"My stomach dropped the second I saw him, Wasim. I didn't even think."
"But you're thinking now. Ammi always says the first thought comes by itself; the second one is yours."
"Yeah. Next time I'll catch the first one."

qa.q: What did the man say when he gave back the purse?
qa.a: He said, "Didi, your stuff," and then he just left.

qa.q: What is Afreen feeling after she gets home, and why?
qa.a: She feels ashamed and uneasy, because she had decided the man was a thief from his clothes alone, and he turned out to be kind.

qa.q: What does Afreen plan to do next time, and why is it a good start?
qa.a: She plans to catch her first thought when it comes; spotting a snap judgment honestly, without beating herself up, leaves room for a fairer second thought.

qa.q: How might the man on the platform have felt if he had noticed Afreen moving her bag away?
qa.a: He might have felt judged or hurt, yet he still ran after her with the purse, which shows how little his clothes said about him.

grounding: Shows a young adult catching her snap judgment of a stranger from his dress and noticing it honestly without harsh self-blame.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage:
"Uma, you take the regression part. You're from Chennai, maths is basically in your blood."
"Ankita, I actually wanted the survey design."
"Come on, you'll finish the numbers in an hour. We'd take a week."
"I scraped through stats last semester."
"Stop being modest!"
"I'm not being modest. I studied every night and still got a C. When everyone says it's in my blood, I feel like I'm not allowed to be stuck."
"Oh. I thought I was complimenting you."
"I know you did. It's just, if I mess up, it's like I've let down a whole city."
"That's heavy. Sorry, Uma. So, survey design?"
"Survey design. And can we split the regression? I'll need help with it."
"Deal. Honestly, I'm terrible at it too."
"Good. Then we'll be terrible together."

qa.q: What grade did Uma get in stats last semester?
qa.a: Uma studied every night and still got a C.

qa.q: Why does Ankita's praise weigh on Uma?
qa.a: Uma feels pressured and anxious, as if being called a natural at maths leaves no room to be stuck or to fail.

qa.q: How did Uma correct the praise without hurting the friendship?
qa.a: Uma calmly shared the real grade and how the label felt, then asked to split the regression, so Ankita could see a person rather than a type.

qa.q: How does Ankita see the comment about Chennai at first?
qa.a: Ankita thinks it is a compliment and is surprised it adds pressure, then apologises and admits to finding regression hard too.

grounding: Shows a young adult praised as naturally good at maths because of where they come from, feeling unable to fail, and kindly correcting it.
